INSERT INTO blog_posts (title, slug, category, excerpt, content, publishedAt) VALUES 
('Right to Counsel: What Landlords Need to Know About Opposing Funded Attorneys', 'right-to-counsel-opposing-funded-attorneys', 'Legal Compliance', 'Washington is the first state in the nation to guarantee legal representation for low-income tenants in eviction proceedings. Learn how the Right to Counsel program works, who qualifies, and how it impacts your eviction timeline and strategy.', 'Washington is the first state in the nation to guarantee legal representation for low-income tenants in eviction proceedings. That milestone happened in 2021. What has taken longer to filter into landlord operations is the practical reality of what it means to go to court when the other side has a funded, trained attorney. If you are managing rental properties in Washington today, this is not a policy issue, it is a case management issue.

This article explains how the Right to Counsel program works, who qualifies, what it does to your timeline, and how to adjust your approach accordingly.

## How the Program Works

Senate Bill 5160, signed into law in April 2021, created RCW 59.18.640, which requires Washington courts to appoint counsel for indigent tenants in unlawful detainer proceedings. The program is administered through Northwest Justice Project and a network of legal aid providers statewide. Funding flows through the Washington State Supreme Court's Access to Justice Board and, in recent years, through direct legislative appropriations.

The statute defines "indigent" broadly. Any tenant who receives a means-tested public benefit, such as TANF, SSI, food assistance, or Medicaid, automatically qualifies. So does any tenant whose post-tax annual income is at or below 200 percent of the federal poverty level. That threshold covers a significant portion of the renter population in most Washington markets. Do not assume your tenant won't qualify because they were working. The income test alone captures a wide range.

If an eligible tenant appears in court without an attorney, the court is required to delay the proceeding until counsel can be arranged should the tenant request such. The eviction does not move forward without it.

## What the Numbers Actually Show

Since the program launched in 2022, more than 30,000 tenants have received representation. Advocates report that 90 percent of closed cases resulted in tenants remaining in their homes or securing alternative permanent housing. Only 15 percent of cases ended in an eviction judgment for the landlord. The program's own data shows that 27 percent of cases resolved with a negotiated move-out agreement and 15 percent with the tenant remaining under a repayment arrangement.

Those numbers get cited frequently in policy debates. What they mean operationally is this: when a tenant has a competent attorney, default judgments effectively disappear, procedural defects get identified and litigated, and settlement pressure on landlords increases substantially. The landlord who shows up to an unlawful detainer hearing expecting a fast default against an unrepresented tenant will encounter a different proceeding than they anticipated.

## What It Does to Your Timeline

Before right-to-counsel implementation, straightforward nonpayment cases in many Washington counties resolved at show cause in four to six weeks from notice service. That benchmark no longer holds in markets where program capacity is highest, primarily King, Pierce, and Snohomish counties.

Two things extend timelines under the current program. First, if an eligible tenant is unrepresented when the case is called, the court must continue the hearing to arrange counsel. In high-volume courts, that continuance can add weeks. Second, once counsel is appointed, defense attorneys frequently request additional continuances to prepare, gather financial records, or pursue pre-litigation resolution. Courts generally grant them.

The practical result in King County is that contested nonpayment cases often run four to six months from initiation to resolution. Simpler cases may resolve faster. Cases with any procedural issue in the notice or filing such an incorrect notice period, a defective service method, a noncompliant notice form, take longer, because defense counsel knows how to find those issues and use them.

Right now in 2026, the program is under budget pressure. Governor Ferguson's supplemental budget includes $3 million in continued funding. Without it, advocacy groups estimate 17 attorney positions statewide would be eliminated. If the program contracts, coverage gaps may reappear in smaller counties. Watch this if you operate in Cowlitz, Lewis, or Grays Harbor Counties, as these are markets where program capacity has historically been thinner.

## How to Prepare When the Other Side Has a Lawyer

The presence of defense counsel on the other side changes the case, but it does not change the law. RCW 59.18 has not been amended to favor tenants simply because they have representation. What changes is the consequences of imprecision.

Your notice has to be right the first time. Defense attorneys in right-to-counsel cases routinely challenge notice content, service method, and the statutory basis cited. A 14-day pay or vacate notice that uses the wrong statutory language, fails to include the required itemization, or was served by a method that cannot be documented will not survive motion practice. Get the notice right, document the service, and retain your proof of service.

Your grounds have to match your documentation. If you are evicting for nonpayment, the amount stated in the notice must match your ledger exactly. If you are evicting for a lease violation, the written violation must be documented in writing and the cure period must have been properly calculated and allowed to run. Experienced defense counsel will pull the ledger, pull the lease, and identify any gap between what your notice says and what your records show.

Expect the show cause hearing to be contested. In jurisdictions where the Right to Counsel program is operating, show cause hearings frequently involve argument, exhibits, and legal memoranda. Coming in with nothing but verbal representations of what happened is not adequate preparation in that environment.

Resolution offers are not weakness. Some nonpayment cases are better resolved through a stipulated payment agreement than pushed through contested litigation. This is true whether or not the tenant has a lawyer. What the presence of defense counsel changes is that the tenant now has someone advising them on what to accept. Offers need to be structured and documented correctly to be enforceable.

## The Quinn Posner Perspective

I work regularly with Washington's Right to Counsel program, not in opposition to it as a policy matter, but as a practical reality of eviction practice. The program has been operating statewide since 2022. It has changed the texture of unlawful detainer practice in this state. Landlords who prepared for that change are managing it. Landlords who are still operating as if evictions work the way they did in 2019 are losing cases they should be winning.

The legal standard for eviction has not changed. RCW 59.18.650 still defines the grounds. The notice requirements are still the notice requirements. What has changed is that a growing percentage of the tenants on the other side of your case have counsel who knows those requirements as well as you do, or better.

The answer is not panic. The answer is precision. Notices served correctly, grounds documented properly, and an attorney on your side who has been in these hearings and knows what to expect.', '2026-05-18 00:00:00'),

('City-Specific Ordinance Landmines: Seattle, Tacoma, and Beyond', 'city-specific-ordinance-landmines-seattle-tacoma', 'Legal Compliance', 'Washington's Residential Landlord-Tenant Act sets the floor, not the ceiling. Discover the local ordinances in Seattle, Tacoma, and Vancouver that create additional requirements beyond state law and can sink your eviction if ignored.', 'Washington's Residential Landlord-Tenant Act (RCW 59.18) sets the floor. It does not set the ceiling. Across Washington's major cities, local ordinances have built a second layer of requirements, including longer notice periods, additional fee restrictions, mandatory registrations, and eviction bans that have no analog in state law. If you're managing properties in more than one Washington city and your compliance program treats state law as the complete picture, you are operating on incomplete information.

This article covers the most consequential city-level overlays in Seattle, Tacoma, and Vancouver, Washington. It is not an exhaustive survey. It is the list of requirements that are most likely to sink an eviction, create penalty exposure, or generate tenant litigation if ignored.

## Seattle: Five Layers You Don't Have in Other Jurisdictions

Seattle has more local landlord-tenant regulation than any other Washington city. Each layer operates independently. Violating one does not excuse compliance with another.

### 180-Day Rent Increase Notice

State law (HB 1217) requires 90 days' written notice before a rent increase. Seattle requires 180 days, twice the state minimum. This requirement predates HB 1217 and was not superseded by it. If you serve a 90-day notice on a Seattle tenant, you have served a defective notice. The notice is unenforceable, you must reissue it, and you have given the tenant an additional 90 days by mistake.

Seattle also requires that rent increase notices include specific City language directing tenants to contact "Renting in Seattle" for tenant rights information. Notices without that language are treated as defective, regardless of how much advance notice was given.

### Economic Displacement Relocation Assistance (EDRA)

Any housing cost increase notice issued on or after July 1, 2022, that equals or exceeds 10 percent within a 12-month period triggers EDRA. You must attach the EDRA notice to the increase notice itself. The EDRA requirement does not exist in state law. It is a Seattle overlay that most landlords and a surprising number of practitioners miss.

### Rental Registration and Inspection Ordinance (RRIO)

Every rental unit in Seattle must be registered under RRIO, renewed every two years, and inspected on a rotating schedule. Registration costs $126 per property plus $31.50 per additional unit. Failure to maintain current RRIO registration is not just a code violation. It can prevent you from pursuing an eviction even when your legal grounds are solid. Noncompliance creates a procedural vulnerability your tenant's attorney will find immediately.

### Fair Chance Housing (SMC 14.09)

Seattle's Fair Chance Housing Ordinance broadly restricts the use of criminal history in tenant screening. Landlords cannot require applicants to disclose criminal history, and cannot take adverse action based on most conviction records. Following a 2023 Ninth Circuit ruling (Yim v. City of Seattle), the Seattle Office for Civil Rights no longer enforces the inquiry ban, but it continues to enforce the adverse action prohibitions. You can run a background check. You generally cannot act on what you find. If your PM company uses criminal history as a routine screening filter, that practice creates liability in Seattle that it does not create in most other jurisdictions.

The ordinance permits adverse action based on sex offender registry information for adult applicants, provided the landlord can demonstrate a legitimate business reason. Registry-based adverse action is prohibited entirely for juvenile applicants or where the conviction occurred when the individual was a juvenile.

## Tacoma: Ordinance 29086 and the Landlord Fairness Code Initiative

Tacoma passed Ordinance 29086 in late 2025, amending its Rental Housing Code (TMC 1.95) and adding the Landlord Fairness Code Initiative (TMC 1.100). Both took effect January 1, 2026. The combination creates obligations that significantly exceed state law requirements.

### Relocation Assistance Triggered by Rent Increases

Under the Landlord Fairness Code Initiative, any rent increase of 5 percent or more within a 12-month period triggers mandatory relocation assistance if the tenant requests it. The amount scales with the size of the increase:

- Increases of 5% or more (up to 7.5%): two months' rent
- Increases over 7.5% (up to 10%): two and a half months' rent
- Increases over 10%: three months' rent

The landlord has 30 days to pay after receiving the tenant's request. A tenant in a $1,800/month unit receiving a 6% increase can request $3,600. If the tenant requests assistance and then does not relocate, they must repay within 10 days. State law contains no equivalent requirement.

Three exemptions apply: the obligation does not apply where the landlord and tenant live on the same site and the site has four or fewer dwelling units; where the tenant has lived in the unit for less than six months; or where the landlord is temporarily renting out their principal residence during an absence due to active-duty military service.

The practical consequence for PM companies with Tacoma portfolios is that every rent increase decision now has to be modeled against the relocation assistance exposure. An increase that looks modest on paper can produce a significant per-unit liability if a meaningful percentage of eligible tenants opt to relocate.

### Three Separate Eviction Protection Layers

Ordinance 29086 creates three categories of eviction protection, each operating independently.

The school-year defense (TMC 1.100.060) applies when an eviction would require a tenant to vacate during the school year and the tenant or any resident is a child or student, a person with legal custody of a child or student, or an educator.

The cold-weather prohibition (TMC 1.100.063) bars evictions between November 15 and March 15. One exception applies: landlords who own four or fewer rental units within Tacoma city limits are exempt from the cold-weather ban.

The status-based eviction prohibition (TMC 1.100.070) is a separate layer entirely. It bars evictions based on a tenant's status as a service member, first responder, senior, family member, health care provider, or educator. It also bars eviction based solely on a tenant's immediate family members residing in the unit, absent a violation of applicable occupancy limits.

Under TMC 1.100.065, the school-year and cold-weather protections do not apply where the eviction basis is waste, nuisance, or illegal activity; owner or family occupancy of the unit; sale of the unit; condemnation; removal of a roommate; or sexual harassment by the tenant. The status-based prohibition under 1.100.070 does not have these same carveouts.

None of these protections exist in RCW 59.18. Filing in Tacoma without first reviewing which category the tenant falls into, and whether an exception applies, means filing blind.

### Compliance Prerequisites for Evictions and Rent Increases

A Tacoma landlord cannot pursue an eviction or increase rent without a current City of Tacoma business license, or if the unit has defective conditions making it uninhabitable under RCW 59.18.060. An expired license or unresolved code violation is an immediate, correctable obstacle. It is also the first thing experienced tenant-side attorneys check.

## Vancouver, Washington: Mandatory Rental Registration

Beginning January 1, 2026, all residential rental units in Vancouver, Washington, must be registered with the City. This requirement applies to all rental housing, from single-family homes to large multifamily properties. Operating an unregistered rental unit violates the Vancouver Municipal Code.

For PM companies with properties in Clark County that straddle Vancouver's city limits and unincorporated county areas, this creates an administrative distinction that needs to be built into your compliance calendar. Units inside Vancouver carry a recurring registration obligation. Units in unincorporated Clark County do not.

## Spokane: A Just Cause Ordinance Under Consideration

Spokane is actively considering a just cause eviction ordinance that would restrict the grounds on which landlords can terminate month-to-month tenancies. As of this writing, no ordinance has passed. If Spokane adopts just cause protections, it would join a growing list of Washington cities that have expanded beyond RCW 59.18's termination framework. That is worth monitoring now. PM companies with Spokane portfolios should be tracking city council activity now, not after passage.

## The Compliance Architecture Problem

The practical challenge for enterprise PM companies is not any single ordinance. It is the compounding effect of tracking several independent regulatory frameworks simultaneously. Your Seattle properties need a 180-day rent increase calendar, RRIO registration tracking, and Fair Chance Housing screening protocols. Your Tacoma properties need a business license verification step, a relocation assistance calculator embedded in every increase decision, and a three-layer eviction review before any unlawful detainer is filed. Your Vancouver properties need a registration audit.

None of these requirements are optional, and none of them are self-executing. They require deliberate compliance architecture: someone who knows which rules apply in which jurisdiction and has built them into the workflow before the situation arises, not after an eviction is already challenged.

Outside counsel who practices only in their home county and tracks only RCW 59.18 is a liability in this environment. The city-level overlay is not a footnote to Washington landlord-tenant law. For multi-jurisdictional PM companies, it is a substantial portion of the practical compliance burden.', '2026-05-11 00:00:00')
